gaps: No study found linking stretched necklines, worn cuffs, fading or pilling to personality, habits or job.
No reliable source found for reading someone’s job from wear patterns.
Hughes’ and Van Edwards’ views on clothes are practitioner opinion, not tested profiling.
Body-odour studies mostly use small samples and lab sniff tests.

items.title: The Behaviour Expert: Instantly Read Any Room
items.get: Chase on how to read a room: slow down, notice posture and appearance, and look for what has changed from a person’s normal.

items.title: Body Language Expert: Stop Using This
items.get: Vanessa on the cues that make you come across as warm and capable, and the small habits that quietly put people off.

items.title: Body Language Expert Explains Why People Dislike You
items.get: A first-impressions conversation, with sunglasses as one everyday example of a cue that gets in the way.

items.title: How To Overcome Awkwardness
items.get: A long chat about easing awkwardness: posture, eye contact, tone of voice and what to do with your hands.

items.title: This Speaking Mistake Makes People Dislike You
items.get: Vinh on how your delivery and body language land, with a look at how clothes, hair and glasses add to the picture.

items.title: Simple rule for using hand gestures
items.get: One easy rule for your hands: keep them in the band between your belly button and your eyes.

items.title: Your body language may shape who you are
items.get: Amy Cuddy on whether holding an open, expansive posture can change how confident you feel.
items.note: Some of the findings in this talk are disputed, and TED says so on the video. Treat power posing as something to try, not a proven fix.

items.title: Color Psychology: How Color Choices Affect Behavior
items.get: Vanessa on how the colours you wear can send a mood message, and how colour can affect stress and mood.

items.title: How Appearance Affects Success
items.get: Joe Navarro on how dress and appearance feed into the impression of success, money and power.

items.title: Styling from Inside Out
items.get: A TEDx talk on fashion psychology: how what you put on can change how you feel inside.

items.title: USask Research Minute
items.get: A short research summary on how a psychologist’s visible tattoos change what prospective clients assume.

items.title: What do your clothes say about you?
items.get: A short animation on how people use clothes to say who they are.

items.title: The Psychology of Black Hair
items.get: A TEDx talk on how Black hair is read in first impressions, with the bias and identity that come with it.

items.title: Yes, grooming does matter!
items.get: A quick tip on how grooming and presentation shape a first impression.

items.title: Shoes tell of your inner sole?
items.get: A short news segment on research suggesting shoes may say more about the wearer than you would expect.

items.title: Leaving a Footprint
items.get: A TEDx talk about shoes as a story of power, politics and price.

items.title: My formula for self confidence
items.get: A quick routine: practise a confident posture so you feel and sound more sure of yourself.

items.title: Your Body Language Is Talking (Even When You’re Not)
items.get: Joe Navarro on how posture, gestures and facial expressions colour how other people see you.

items.title: BML Walker
items.get: Play with a walking figure made of dots. Slide it between nervous and relaxed, happy and sad, and watch the walk change.

items.title: Biology in Motion
items.get: A short video about Nikolaus Troje’s lab, which studies how we see other people move.

items.title: Johansson: Motion Perception, part 2
items.get: A classic 1971 film showing how a handful of moving dots is enough for us to see a person.

items.title: Biological Motion
items.get: A demo page of dot-only people in motion, where viewers can often judge things like mood.

items.title: What Does Eye Contact Really Do to the Brain?
items.get: A very short take on what eye contact does to the brain. Slim on detail, handy as a prompt.

items.title: What are you looking at? Adventures in human gaze behaviour
items.get: A research talk on where people look and why, and how gaze habits differ from person to person.

items.title: Eye-tracking in the wild and in film
items.get: A research talk on eye-tracking: where viewers look in real scenes and in film.

items.title: The benefits of good posture
items.get: A short animated explainer on why good posture matters for your body.

items.title: 9 tips for a healthy ergonomic workstation
items.get: A clinic ergonomist runs through desk set-up basics that keep your neck, back and wrists comfortable.

items.title: What the power pose controversy reveals about science
items.get: A science channel traces how power posing took off, why it was challenged, and what that says about how research gets tested.

items.title: You can’t fix your posture (here’s why)
items.get: An evidence-minded fitness creator on posture myths and why pain and "bad posture" are less tightly linked than people think.
items.note: A fitness influencer’s take, not a clinical source. Pair it with the NHS back pain page.

items.title: Posture is the loudest form of body language
items.get: A half-minute reminder from Vinh that how you hold yourself speaks before you do.

items.title: Find your primal posture and sit without back pain
items.get: A posture teacher argues that modern sitting and standing habits differ from how people in some cultures move, and shows her fixes.
items.note: Teaching method sold by its creator. Independent evidence is limited.

items.title: How fashion affects your brain
items.get: A short fashion-magazine video on whether wearing a different outfit, like a lab coat, can change how you think and feel.

items.title: How formal clothes can impact our psychology
items.get: A news segment on a study linking formal clothing to a more big-picture way of thinking.

items.title: What your clothes reveal about you
items.get: A short documentary on the unwritten rules of what to wear, and how clothes carry social meaning.

items.title: The psychology of fashion
items.get: A cognitive psychologist talks through how clothes shape mood, identity and the impressions we make.

items.title: Dressed: how to think about clothes
items.get: A university lecture on how to think about clothes, drawing on philosophy and literature.

items.title: Your clothes are literally changing your brain
items.get: A stylist’s explainer on "enclothed cognition", the idea that what you wear shifts how you feel and act.
items.note: A stylist’s read of the research. The evidence on enclothed cognition is mixed.

items.title: How to build a wardrobe you love in 7 steps
items.get: An image consultant’s step-by-step approach to building a wardrobe that feels like you.
items.note: Image-consultant advice. Opinion and experience, not research.

items.title: Why we buy clothes we never wear
items.get: A fashion psychologist on why people hold on to clothes for a "someday" self, and what a wardrobe can reveal.

items.title: The tangled history of Black hair discrimination in the US
items.get: A news explainer on how Black hairstyles have been policed in schools and workplaces, and the pushback against it.

items.title: Johansson: Motion Perception, part 1
items.get: The first part of the classic film showing how a few moving lights are enough to see a person walking.

items.title: Gait recognition
items.get: A UK lab shows how software can match people by how they walk, as a surveillance aid.

items.title: Take an emotion walk
items.get: A research video on teaching a computer to guess perceived emotion from walking style. It guesses what viewers would say, not what someone feels.

items.title: Measuring gait speed for fall risk assessment
items.get: A clinical video on timing a short walk to help judge falls risk. Walking speed is a health measure, not a personality cue.
items.note: Health context: if someone’s walking has changed, suggest they see a GP.

items.title: Gait impairments in Parkinson’s disease
items.get: A short clinical video on the kinds of walking changes seen as Parkinson’s progresses.
items.note: Not a diagnosis tool. If you’re worried about someone, suggest they see a GP.

items.title: Does color really affect how you act?
items.get: A science channel checks the popular claims about colour and mood, and why the evidence is less tidy than the internet makes it sound.

items.title: The physics and psychology of colour
items.get: A Royal Institution talk using demos and illusions to show how much of colour is made by our own perception.

items.title: Should you trust your first impression?
items.get: A short animation on how fast we judge strangers, and when those snap judgements help or mislead.

items.title: Body language expert explains how to show confidence
items.get: Joe Navarro walks through poses and habits that look confident, and why some cues work against you.

items.title: What your body odour says about you
items.get: Two hosts and researchers go through what sweat and body odour do and don’t say about a person, with health pointers.
items.note: Health context: a sudden change in someone’s smell can have medical causes. Suggest a GP, not a guess.

items.title: The importance of being inauthentic
items.get: A body-language coach talks about why deliberately shaping your non-verbal signals can land better than just “being yourself”.
items.note: Coaching framework from the speaker. Not peer-reviewed research.

items.title: Physiognomy, explained
items.get: A face-reading channel explains what physiognomy claims and why it is making a comeback.
items.note: Fringe. Reading character from facial features isn’t supported by evidence. Included so you can recognise the claims.

items.title: TikTok’s obsession with face reading and its dark history
items.get: A long video essay on the face-reading trend and the discredited history behind it.
items.note: A creator’s critical essay, not a research source.

items.title: How to find your colour season, for beginners
items.get: An image consultant explains the colour-season idea and how people try to find theirs.
items.note: Season systems aren’t scientifically validated. Treat the result as shopping shorthand, not a verdict.

items.title: Is colour analysis just a scam?
items.get: A stylist who trained in colour analysis explains where she thinks the trend over-promises and what to try instead.
items.note: One stylist’s sceptical opinion. Useful as a counterpoint.

items.title: Science of facial hair: what do beards and stubble signal?
items.get: A men’s-style channel’s take on what beards and stubble signal to other people.
items.note: Style-coach commentary. Not a research source.

items.title: How to have good posture and walk elegantly (deportment)
items.get: An etiquette coach’s lesson in the old deportment tradition: how to stand and walk with poise.
items.note: Etiquette coaching. Opinion and tradition, not research.

items.title: Dress is a fundamental component of person perception
items.get: A review arguing that clothes, hair and accessories shape first impressions, and sorting what people infer from them: group, state of mind, status and taste.

items.title: What to wear when: outfits and first impressions of job applicants
items.get: Raters judged a drawn woman in 12 outfits for different jobs. Fitted and layered looks scored better, and what counted as right depended on the job.
items.note: An older, small study with drawings, so use it as a nudge, not a rule.

items.title: Allison Bornstein’s tips for finding your personal style
items.get: A stylist’s "three-word" method: pick a practical, an aspirational and an emotional word to steer what you wear and buy.
items.note: Style-press advice. Opinion and experience, not research.

items.title: Clothing aesthetics: colour choices to match fair and tanned skin
items.get: Observers matched cool blues to fair skin and warm orange-reds to tanned skin. The authors note stylists’ season categories aren’t defined scientifically.

items.title: Color psychology: effects of perceiving color on psychological functioning
items.get: A scholarly review of what colour does to mood and behaviour, and where the evidence is still thin.

items.title: The false promise of seasonal-colour analysis
items.get: A critical long read arguing the season trend borrows the language of colour science without the proof.

items.title: How to find the colours that are perfect for you
items.get: A BBC look at the colour-analysis boom, mostly through consultants and clients who say it changed how they feel.
items.note: Reports on colour analysis, which isn’t scientifically validated. Mostly practitioners’ own accounts.

items.title: Seasonal colour analysis explained: history and evidence
items.get: A colour-analysis app’s blog sorts what is supported (colours near your face change how skin looks) from what is untested (that your palette flatters you more).
items.note: Written by a company selling colour analysis. Read the evidence section critically.

items.title: Colour Me Beautiful (UK)
items.get: The long-running image-consultancy brand behind the "season" idea. Useful to see how colour analysis is sold.
items.note: Commercial site. Season systems aren’t scientifically validated.

items.title: Hairstyle as an adaptive means of displaying phenotypic quality
items.get: Tests how six hairstyles, from long and tidy to unkempt, change how attractive a face is rated.

items.title: Facial hair and perceptions of men
items.get: Looks at how beards and stubble change women’s ratings of men’s attractiveness, health, masculinity and parenting ability.

items.title: The natural hair bias in job recruitment
items.get: Four studies found a hiring bias against Black women wearing natural hairstyles.

items.title: Hair loss
items.get: The NHS guide to why hair thins or falls out and when it is worth seeing a GP.
items.note: If you’re worried about someone, suggest they see a GP. Don’t guess at causes.

items.title: Body odour (BO)
items.get: The NHS guide to common causes of body odour, what helps, and when to see a GP.
items.note: Smell can have medical causes. If you’re worried about someone, suggest they see a GP.

items.title: Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)
items.get: The NHS page on heavy sweating that doesn’t fit the situation, and when to get help.
items.note: If someone sweats a lot, it may be a treatable condition. Suggest a GP, not a verdict.

items.title: The search for human pheromones: the lost decades
items.outlet: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
items.get: A review finding no solid evidence for the "human pheromones" often claimed. Humans may have them, but they haven’t been shown.

items.title: Chemosignals communicate human emotions
items.get: A lab study testing whether smelling sweat from people in different emotional states nudges the sniffer’s own expression.
items.note: Small lab study. One piece of the picture.

items.title: Shoes as a source of first impressions
items.get: Strangers rated owners from photos of their shoes alone. Some basics like age and income came through, with limits.

items.title: Shoes reveal personality traits
items.get: A short write-up of the shoe study. Observers beat chance on age, gender, income and attachment anxiety, but caught only about half of the real cues.

items.title: Do slumped and upright postures affect stress responses?
items.get: A randomised trial comparing slumped and upright sitting during a stressful task, measuring mood and self-esteem.

items.title: Body posture effects on self-evaluation
items.who: Pablo Briñol, Richard Petty and Benjamin Wagner
items.get: Sitting upright made people more confident in the good or bad things they wrote about themselves.

items.title: Power posing: P-curving the evidence
items.get: A statistical re-look at the power-posing literature, finding little real evidence in it.

items.title: P-curving a more comprehensive body of research on postural feedback
items.who: Amy Cuddy, Stephen Schultz and Nathan Fosse
items.get: The power-posing side’s reply, arguing a broader set of studies shows an effect on feelings.
items.note: One side of an open debate. Read it with the Simmons paper.

items.title: Expansive and contractive postures: a review and meta-analysis
items.get: Pooled 73 studies: slumped, closed postures worsen mood, but open postures add little over a neutral one.

items.title: "Sit up straight": time to re-evaluate
items.outlet: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
items.get: Physiotherapy researchers question the belief that "bad posture" causes spinal pain.

items.title: Can power posing make you feel more confident?
items.get: A plain-English summary: effects on feeling are stronger than on hormones or behaviour, and may come from avoiding slumping.

items.title: Back pain
items.get: NHS advice on back pain, including staying active, and when to see a GP.
items.note: If someone is in ongoing pain, suggest a GP or physio. Don’t blame posture by sight.

items.title: Alexander technique lessons, exercise and massage for back pain
items.get: A UK trial where one-to-one Alexander technique lessons eased long-term back pain more than usual care.

items.title: The Alexander Technique
items.who: Society of Teachers of the Alexander Technique
items.get: The UK teachers’ society explains the technique, a way of changing habits of posture and movement.
items.note: Complementary practice. The trial above is the main independent evidence.

items.title: Gokhale Method
items.get: The posture teacher’s own site, covering her "primal posture" approach to sitting, standing and walking.
items.note: Method sold by its creator. Independent evidence is limited.

items.title: Decomposing biological motion
items.get: The paper behind the BML Walker: how a walk can be split into dimensions such as sex, weight and mood.

items.title: Recognising the sex of a walker from a point-light display
items.get: A classic study showing observers can often tell a walker’s sex from dots alone.

items.title: The identification of emotions from gait information
items.get: Observers read emotions such as sadness and anger from how people walk.

items.title: First impressions: gait cues drive reliable trait judgements
items.get: Observers agree with each other on traits seen in walking, but agreement isn’t the same as accuracy.

items.title: Gait patterns associated with sadness and depression
items.get: Compared the walking of people with depression with others, and of people induced to feel sad.
items.note: Research on groups, not a way to spot depression. If you’re worried about someone’s mood, ask kindly and suggest a GP.

items.title: Gait speed and survival in older adults
items.get: Pooled data from older adults: walking speed tracked closely with how long people went on to live.
items.note: A population finding. It says nothing reliable about one person you see walking.

items.title: Foot drop
items.get: NHS guide to difficulty lifting the front of the foot, a cause of changed walking, and when to see a GP.
items.note: If someone’s walking has changed, suggest they see a GP. Don’t guess the cause.

items.title: Falls
items.get: NHS advice on falls and unsteadiness, what raises the risk and when to ask for help.
items.note: If someone seems unsteady or has fallen, suggest they see a GP.

items.title: Social attributions from faces
items.get: A review of how quickly we judge faces, how much we agree, and how limited their accuracy is.

items.title: Physiognomy
items.get: A neutral overview of face reading: its history, its use in racist pseudoscience, and why scientists reject it.

items.title: Biological motion
items.get: White dots that look random until the film plays, then a walking figure appears. A neat way to feel how little it takes to see a person.

items.title: Teachable Machine
items.get: Train a model in your browser to tell two postures apart from your webcam. Shows how posture-detection software learns.

items.title: GaitSet
items.get: Code for a well-known network that recognises people by their walking silhouettes, from different camera angles.

items.title: OpenGait
items.get: A toolbox that collects several gait-recognition methods and datasets under one roof.

items.title: STEP: emotion from gait
items.get: Code behind the "Take an Emotion Walk" research on guessing perceived emotion from skeleton walks.
items.note: Predicts what viewers would perceive, not what a person feels.

items.title: Sitting posture detection (YOLOv5)
items.get: A small open project that flags good and bad sitting posture from a side-on webcam view.
items.note: Posture labels here are the author’s own rules, not clinical advice.

items.title: OpenPose
items.get: The widely used system that finds body, hand and face keypoints in video. A building block for posture and gait tools.

items.title: DeepFashion
items.get: A large clothing-image dataset with labels for garment type and attributes, used in fashion research.

items.title: CelebAMask-HQ
items.get: A face-image dataset with labelled regions such as hair, used to train hair and face segmentation.

items.title: If you only have a full-length photo of someone…
items.get: Strangers can still read some of their more outgoing, visible traits from it. This works best for obvious traits and varies a lot between people.

items.title: If someone wears a suit rather than sweatpants…
items.get: They may act more dominant. In a negotiation, suit-wearers took more of the profit, and the other person grew more watchful.

items.title: If someone is dressed formally…
items.get: They may think in a more big-picture way, tied to feeling powerful. A correction was issued for this paper, so treat it lightly.

items.title: If clothes seem to change how the wearer thinks (“enclothed cognition”)…
items.get: The evidence is mixed. The famous white-coat result didn’t replicate, but studies after 2015 look more solid.

items.title: If someone breaks the dress code on purpose (red trainers at work, gym kit in a luxury shop)…
items.get: People may see them as higher in status and competence. It only works when it looks deliberate and the observer knows the norms.

items.title: If someone wears visible luxury labels…
items.get: One study found they were treated better, but a stricter double-blind replication found no effect.

items.title: If someone stands tall in smart clothes…
items.get: Posture and clothing combine in how competent they look, and the mix differs for men and women.

items.title: If someone dresses like their peers…
items.get: A practitioner guide reads it as a sign of a conformity driver. It is a coaching view, not a tested test.

items.title: If someone turns up in clean clothes again and again…
items.get: Joe Navarro says it builds trust through consistency, and that people tend to prefer the well-groomed and well-dressed.
items.note: A practitioner’s view on a major outlet, not a tested finding.

items.title: If you form a view from a very short clip of behaviour…
items.get: Short clips can predict some real outcomes. That is not the same as reading a whole person.

items.title: If you smell someone’s untreated sweat…
items.get: In one study, men rated women as less confident and competent while smelling it. Smell can colour judgement without you noticing.

items.title: If someone’s hygiene slips, they lose weight or wear the same clothes every day…
items.get: These appear in UK abuse and neglect indicator lists. They are prompts to ask kindly, not verdicts. If you’re worried, suggest they speak to a GP or follow your safeguarding route. SCIE also warns against judging someone’s cleanliness or lifestyle.

items.title: If a suit fits better, or a small detail is neater…
items.get: In one study the same man in a better-cut suit was rated more confident, successful and better paid. Trustworthiness barely moved.

items.title: If someone wears a uniform or formal dress…
items.get: Classic field studies found people complied more. That is about status and role, not a personality profile.
items.note: Strength not rated in the research file.

items.title: If someone is wearing red…
items.get: Don’t read much into it. An early study found red raised attractiveness ratings, but two preregistered replications found very weak, uncertain effects.

items.title: If clothes or armpits smell stale or sour…
items.get: Skin bacteria have usually broken down the sweat. Fresh sweat has very little smell of its own.

items.title: If the smell is sulphurous or onion-like…
items.get: That fits the sulphur compounds underarm bacteria make from sweat.

items.title: If a polyester top smells worse than a cotton one after the same workout…
items.get: Part of it is the fabric. Polyester shirts smelled stronger and less pleasant, and grew different bacteria.

items.title: If a synthetic garment still smells after washing…
items.get: Polyester can hold on to odour even after laundering. Fabrics that soak up less water tend to give off more smell.

items.title: If clean laundry smells like a damp, dirty dishcloth…
items.get: It may have dried slowly indoors. One bacterium (Moraxella osloensis) makes that smell and survives drying.

items.title: If someone smells of stale smoke but doesn’t smoke…
items.get: Smoke chemicals cling to clothes and skin and are given off indoors afterwards, so it may just be where they have been.

items.title: If someone has body odour…
items.get: It can come from exercise, hot weather, hormone changes, being overweight, some medicines or some illnesses. The NHS says the cause is often unknown, so don’t assume.

items.title: If someone’s usual smell changes, or they suddenly sweat far more…
items.get: The NHS says to see a GP. A fruity smell can sometimes go with diabetes, and a bleach-like one with liver or kidney problems. Suggest a GP kindly; don’t guess a cause.

items.title: If someone is fighting an infection…
items.get: Their body odour can turn more unpleasant within hours. This comes from lab studies, not something to diagnose by nose.

items.title: Some illnesses have their own smell…
items.get: Parkinson’s changes the make-up of skin oil in lab work. This is research, not something to read by nose.

items.title: If a greasy, grassy body smell is noticed…
items.get: One study found a chemical behind it (2-nonenal) only in people aged 40 and over. Weak evidence; don’t guess ages from smell.

items.title: If someone eats a lot of red meat…
items.get: Their body odour was rated less pleasant in one small study.

items.title: If someone has almost no underarm smell…
items.get: It can be genetic. A gene variant common among many people of Asian ancestry nearly removes typical underarm odour.

items.title: If you try to guess personality from someone’s smell…
items.get: Strangers did only slightly better than chance for extraversion, neuroticism and dominance. Not a reliable cue.

items.title: If an athlete wears red…
items.get: Across several contact sports they won a bit more often. English football teams in red also had a better home record.

items.title: If a man wears red…
items.get: People tend to rate him as more aggressive and dominant, and to read his face as angrier.

items.title: If a team wears black…
items.get: It tends to get more penalties. Referees judged black-clad players more harshly, and the players played more aggressively.

items.title: If someone wears red or black…
items.get: They may be rated as more attractive, and part of this showed even when the colour was hidden. That hints the colour changes how the wearer holds themselves.

items.title: If a woman’s dating-profile photo shows red…
items.get: One set of studies linked it to more interest in casual sex. Weak and context-bound; don’t read a person from it.

items.title: The idea that women wear red or pink at peak fertility…
items.get: It has not held up reliably in later, larger studies.

items.title: Grey, yellow and mood…
items.get: In a colour-wheel study, people with anxious or depressed mood picked grey most often and people with normal mood picked yellow. This was about choosing colours, not clothes.

items.title: Vanessa Van Edwards on colour in clothes…
items.get: Her coaching view is that blue reads as trustworthy, black as authority, grey as neutral or passive, and red as energetic.
items.note: A coaching view, not tested profiling.

items.title: Joe Navarro on colour and rank…
items.get: He notes that in history some colours were reserved by rank, such as purple for kings.
items.note: A practitioner’s remark, not a tested finding.

items.title: If trousers bag at the knees or sleeves at the elbows…
items.get: Repeated, long-lasting force from those joints has deformed the fabric, which points to long or repeated wear.

items.title: If someone’s clothes are worn out…
items.get: It can mean money is tight. Being unable to replace worn-out clothes is an official EU measure of deprivation.

items.title: Why people keep or drop clothes…
items.get: Wear and tear, poor fit, fashion and boredom all play a part, so one worn item says little.

items.title: If someone’s clothes, belt or jewellery look looser over time…
items.get: The NHS lists this among signs of malnutrition, and unplanned weight loss can come from stress or illness. Ask kindly and suggest a GP if you’re worried.

items.title: If you notice a bigger clothing size…
items.get: It tracks a bigger waist and BMI, and with them higher heart and diabetes risk on average. This is a population finding; never comment on someone’s body.

items.title: If you look at someone’s everyday shoes…
items.get: Strangers guessed their age, gender, income and attachment anxiety better than chance.

items.title: If clothes look “richer” or “poorer”…
items.get: The same face is judged more or less competent, even in a flash and even when people are told to ignore the clothes.

items.title: When people read someone’s dress…
items.get: Across 109 older studies they mainly judged four things: how good the person seems, how powerful, how lively, and how they think.

items.title: If someone wears expensive, flashy clothes and looks neat and carefully prepared…
items.get: It can go with higher narcissism. Snap judgements from full-body photos picked this up.
